# Overview

@meadows2001 is a reflective essay in which Donella Meadows shares
practical wisdom for working with complex systems. Rather than trying to
control or predict systems, she argues that we should learn to "dance"
with them — observing, adapting, and working in harmony with their
inherent dynamics.

The paper is available at:
<https://demorrison.ucdavis.edu/files/Meadows_Systems_Thinking_2001.pdf>

# What Is a System?

A **system** is a set of elements interconnected in such a way that they
produce their own pattern of behavior over time. Systems are
characterized by:

- **Elements**: the visible parts of a system (people, trees, water,
  money)
- **Interconnections**: the relationships that hold the elements together
  (flows of information, physical flows, rules)
- **Function or purpose**: what the system does, often not what it
  appears to do

## Stocks and Flows

- A **stock** is any quantity that accumulates or depletes over time
  (water in a bathtub, population, money in a bank account)
- A **flow** is the rate of change of a stock (birth rate, spending
  rate, water flow)

Systems change through their stocks; stocks create inertia and memory.

## Feedback Loops

A **feedback loop** exists when a change in a stock affects the flows
into or out of that same stock.

- **Reinforcing (positive) loops**: amplify change (growth or collapse)
- **Balancing (negative) loops**: resist change, seek a goal or
  equilibrium

## Why Systems Surprise Us

Systems produce behaviors that are counterintuitive. Common reasons we
fail to understand them:

- We focus on events rather than underlying structure
- We mistake correlation for causation
- We ignore time delays between cause and effect
- We underestimate the role of feedback

# The Fifteen Principles

@meadows2001 offers fifteen practical principles for working effectively
with complex systems. Each principle has its own page:

1. [Get the Beat of the System](meadows-2001/01-get-the-beat.qmd) —
   observe before you act; learn the history and rhythms of the system
2. [Expose Your Mental Models](meadows-2001/02-mental-models.qmd) —
   make implicit assumptions explicit and subject them to scrutiny
3. [Honor, Respect, and Distribute Information](meadows-2001/03-honor-information.qmd) —
   accurate, timely, freely distributed information is the lifeblood of
   systems
4. [Use Language with Care](meadows-2001/04-use-language.qmd) —
   enrich vocabulary with systems concepts; avoid language that obscures
   causal structure
5. [Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable](meadows-2001/05-what-is-important.qmd) —
   resist managing only what you can count
6. [Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems](meadows-2001/06-feedback-policies.qmd) —
   design adaptive, responsive policies rather than fixed rules
7. [Go for the Good of the Whole](meadows-2001/07-good-of-whole.qmd) —
   optimizing subsystems can degrade the whole; keep the system in view
8. [Listen to the Wisdom of the System](meadows-2001/08-wisdom-of-system.qmd) —
   respect self-organizing capacities before overriding them
9. [Locate Responsibility in the System](meadows-2001/09-locate-responsibility.qmd) —
   design systems so that decision-makers experience the consequences of
   their choices
10. [Stay Humble — Stay a Learner](meadows-2001/10-stay-humble.qmd) —
    treat interventions as experiments; monitor and revise
11. [Celebrate Complexity](meadows-2001/11-celebrate-complexity.qmd) —
    diversity and redundancy are sources of resilience, not inefficiency
12. [Expand Time Horizons](meadows-2001/12-expand-time.qmd) —
    short-run fixes are often long-run causes; think across timescales
13. [Defy the Disciplines](meadows-2001/13-defy-discipline.qmd) —
    complex systems cross disciplinary boundaries; so must analysis
14. [Expand the Boundary of Caring](meadows-2001/14-expand-caring.qmd) —
    include distant and future people affected by the system
15. [Don't Erode the Goal of Goodness](meadows-2001/15-goal-of-goodness.qmd) —
    hold fast to genuine goals; resist the drift toward what is merely
    achievable
